summary: Describes message processing and dispatching for SNMP within the SNMP architecture: how messages of different versions are sent to the right processing model, and how PDUs go to the right applications. It also describes the SNMPv3 message processing model. It obsoletes RFC 2272 and was replaced by RFC 3412.

eli5.summary: Like a mailroom, this sorts incoming network-management messages by version and sends each to the right desk.

questions: how does snmp handle multiple protocol versions
how are snmp messages routed to applications
subtitle: How SNMP engines route messages to applications and handle multiple protocol versions.

tldr.problem: SNMP networks support multiple protocol versions (v1, v2, v3) simultaneously, and each version has different message formats and security requirements. Incoming messages must be routed to the correct handler, and applications need a unified interface regardless of version.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2572 defines a message processing layer that sits between the transport and applications. A Dispatcher examines incoming messages, identifies their version, routes them to a version-specific Message Processing Model to extract the payload and apply security, then forwards the resulting PDU to the appropriate application. The SNMPv3 Message Processing Model also defines that version's message format with security flags and parameters.
tldr.outcome: SNMP engines can transparently handle mixed protocol versions and route messages to applications based on context and PDU type. This design was adopted in SNMPv3 but was later updated by RFC 3412.

today: RFC 2572 is a Draft Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 3412. The message processing architecture remains fundamental to SNMP, though implementations follow the updated specification. The model of version-specific processing and dispatcher-based routing has proven effective across SNMP v1, v2c, and v3.

sections.title: The Multi-Version Problem
sections.content:
SNMP began with a simple design, but it evolved through three major versions (v1, v2c, v3), each with its own message format. In real networks, these versions coexist: older systems still send SNMPv1 messages, v2c systems are common for backward compatibility, and SNMPv3 adds modern security features. An SNMP engine running on a single manager or agent must handle all three.

The problem is that each version has different procedures for building messages, extracting information, and applying security. The engine needs a clean way to identify the incoming message version, apply the correct procedure, and hand the result to the requesting application. RFC 2572 defines the architecture that makes this possible.
sections.eli5: Imagine a postal service that handles three different letter formats from different countries, each with different postage rules and addressing systems. You need a sorting center that figures out which format each letter uses, processes it accordingly, and sends it to the right place.

sections.title: The Dispatcher and Message Processing Subsystem
sections.content:
RFC 2572 describes two main components that work together: the Dispatcher and the Message Processing Subsystem. The Dispatcher is the hub. It receives outgoing PDUs from applications and incoming messages from the network. For outgoing messages, the application specifies which Message Processing Model to use (v1, v2c, or v3), and the Dispatcher routes the request to that model. The model builds the message and returns it to the Dispatcher, which sends it to the network.

For incoming messages, the Dispatcher examines the message to determine its version. It then routes the message to the corresponding Message Processing Model to extract and validate the contents. The model returns the PDU and metadata (security context, PDU type, etc.), and the Dispatcher uses this information to route the PDU to the right application.
sections.eli5: The Dispatcher is like a mail sorter. For outgoing mail, it puts letters in the correct format. For incoming mail, it reads the format, opens the envelope the right way, and sends the letter to the correct address.

sections.title: The SNMPv3 Message Format
sections.content:
SNMPv3 messages have a precise structure with several fields. At the top level, there is a msgVersion field (set to 3 for SNMPv3), a msgID to match requests with responses, and a msgMaxSize indicating the largest response the sender can accept. The message also carries msgFlags, a bit field that signals whether authentication is present (authFlag) and whether encryption is in use (privFlag).

The msgSecurityModel field identifies which security method was used (for example, user-based security). The msgSecurityParameters field holds security data like timestamps and nonces, used by the security model to validate authenticity and prevent replays.

The actual management data is wrapped in a scopedPDU, which includes an engine ID and context name to identify where the data applies, plus the PDU itself. If encryption is enabled, the scopedPDU is encrypted.
sections.eli5: An SNMPv3 message is like a sealed envelope with labels. It says who it is from, how big the reply can be, whether it is signed and locked, and what context the message is for. Inside is the actual message.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Messages
sections.content:
When an application wants to send a request, it calls the Dispatcher with a PDU and specifies the target, the desired security model, and the context. The Dispatcher generates a unique message ID and routes the request to the appropriate Message Processing Model. The model encodes the message, coordinates with the security subsystem to add authentication and encryption if requested, and returns the finished message. The Dispatcher then sends it to the network.

On the receiving side, the Dispatcher extracts the message version from the incoming bytes, looks up the appropriate Message Processing Model, and asks it to process the message. The model decodes the message, validates security parameters, and extracts the PDU. The Dispatcher then consults its registration table to determine which application has registered for this combination of engine ID and PDU type, and delivers the PDU to that application.
sections.eli5: Sending is like writing a letter, sealing it, and putting it in the mail. Receiving is like the mail arriving, being verified, opened, and delivered to the person it was addressed to.

sections.title: Security and Context-Based Routing
sections.content:
SNMPv3 adds three levels of security through the security flags. noAuthNoPriv requires neither authentication nor encryption and is least secure. authNoPriv authenticates the message to confirm its origin and that it was not modified, but does not encrypt the data. authPriv requires both authentication and encryption, providing the strongest protection.

The Dispatcher also enforces context-based routing: it combines the engine ID and PDU type to determine the application handler. This ensures that management data for different contexts (for example, different MIB views on the same system) can be routed to different applications. Error handling is built in: if no application has registered for a given combination, the engine generates a report indicating an unknown PDU handler.
sections.eli5: Security levels work like envelopes: unsigned is like a postcard, signed but unencrypted is like a sealed letter, and signed-plus-encrypted is like a sealed letter in a locked box. Context routing makes sure the message gets to the right desk.
